messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajesh, a 75‑year‑old cybersecurity analyst of Indian heritage, had spent most of his adult life hunched over keyboards, his fingers dancing across code while a steady stream of alerts flickered across multiple monitors. The rhythm of his work—predictable, algorithmic—had become a sanctuary, a place where he felt in control. Yet that sense of mastery was shattered in a winter night in 1994, when his son, 14‑year‑old Rahul, collapsed in the school gym, clutching his chest and breathing a ragged, alarmed gasp. The ambulance rushed him to St. Mary’s Hospital, where the sterile antiseptic air seemed to press against Rajesh’s skin, and the fluorescent lights above his son’s head were blindingly bright. In the dim ward, a doctor’s voice—flat, rehearsed—explained that Rahul had an overwhelming infection that could kill within days. Rajesh could feel his own body tremble as the doctor slipped a needle into Rahul’s arm, injecting a lifesaving drug that felt like a second death for the boy. He sat by the bedside, his hands shaking, watching his son’s breathing thin, knowing that every beat of the heart could be the last. The night was suffused with the acrid smell of antiseptics, the echo of distant monitors, and the faint hum of machines that seemed to sing of mortality. The image of that night has since become a source of intense fear, horror, guilt, and shame. Whenever Rajesh encounters a medical procedure—a routine blood draw, a dental filling, or even the mere idea of a future scan—he is immediately flooded with those same overwhelming emotions. The antiseptic scent of a hospital room triggers his heart to pound, his breath to catch, his palms to clammy, as if he were again gripping the edge of a life‑end. The threat of a future crisis, the fear that the same cruel fate might befall another loved one, seems to loom larger with each encounter. The memory of Rahul’s suffering, vivid and relentless, resurfaces as a film that plays in his mind, looping over and over, making it hard for Rajesh to focus on his work. He has come to believe that any mention of illness or any scent of antiseptic is a prelude to a catastrophe, a reminder that he might one day be powerless again. The triggers do not merely awaken his emotional terror; they pull him back into the cinematic replay of that winter night. The smell of antiseptic, the cold fluorescent light, the quiet whir of a machine—each of these elements conjures up the image of Rahul’s face, the trembling of his fingers, the urgent whispers of nurses. Rajesh’s mind, in a desperate attempt to anticipate danger, replays that night with startling clarity. It is not simply a memory; it is a living, breathing horror that feels as present as the fluorescent bulbs that line the corridor. He is unable to articulate the sequence of events without losing his thread, as if the words themselves are too fragile to carry the weight of that terror. The more he tries to explain what happened, the more the details dissolve into a haze of dread and helplessness. In turn, this looping memory feeds the threat that erupts when he encounters any medical scenario. The more vividly Rajesh relives that night, the stronger his negative emotions and physical reactions become. He feels a sense of guilt for not being able to save his son, a shame that stains his sense of self as a provider. When he experiences a flashback—where the hospital room seems to expand around him, the sounds grow louder, the air thicker—his heart races, his muscles tighten, and his breath becomes shallow, as though he is again standing at that bedside. These physical reactivities are not merely reactions; they are a reminder that the threat is alive, that the past has not been laid to rest. The feeling that the nightmare is happening right now rather than a distant echo only deepens his sense of threat, and each subsequent flashback becomes more intense. Rajesh’s job has been a double‑edged sword. On one hand, his role in cybersecurity requires him to monitor systems, to be alert to threats, and to respond calmly. On the other, the very vigilance he displays at work has become a source of stress. When an alarm blares, he worries not only about the security breach but also that it might be a sign of a health crisis looming in his future. His avoidance of routine medical checks, prompted by the fear of being confronted with the antiseptic smell or the thought of an examination, has begun to take a toll on his health. He has missed an annual physical, and his hypertension has worsened, a consequence that now interferes with his ability to focus at work. The tension between his professional responsibilities and his personal trauma has created a vicious cycle that has become increasingly difficult to break. It is this relentless loop of triggers, threat, and memory that has led Rajesh to seek help. The constant internal battle has begun to sap his energy, making his nights restless and his days blurred. He is most afraid that he will be unable to protect those he loves or that he will lose his sense of self in the face of impending danger. Yet he also harbors a quiet hope that, with support, he can reclaim the control he once felt over his environment, to separate the hospital scent from the image of a son in pain, and to regain a future where his mind is not occupied by that unending film of his son’s suffering.
